extracted.intended_audience: students learning complex analysis (advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Statements, definitions, and proof techniques from a complex-analysis textbook chapter (Cauchy theory applications, Runge approximation, Schwarz reflection, residues) used as standards for correct solution/argument construction and for recognizing when standard theorems apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry principle (Theorem 5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f+ and f− are holomorphic in Ω+ and Ω− respectively, extend continuously to I (the interior of Ω∩R), and satisfy f+(x)=f−(x) for all x∈I, then the function f defined by f=f+ on Ω+, f=f− on Ω− and equal on I is holomorphic on all of Ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to glue two holomorphic functions on the two sides of a real-axis boundary into a single holomorphic function on the symmetric domain. Proof uses Morera's theorem: check integrals over triangles, raise edges/vertices off the boundary and let perturbation → 0; split triangles whose interiors intersect the real axis into pieces each having an edge or vertex on I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz reflection principle (Theorem 5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in Ω+ and extends continuously to I and f is real-valued on I, then there exists F holomorphic in all of Ω such that F=f on Ω+ (i.e., f extends across the real axis to the symmetric domain).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the extension on the lower half by reflecting/conjugating values on the real axis (standard construction F(z)=overline{f(overline{z})} on the reflected side). Continuity on I + the symmetry principle ensure holomorphy across I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runge's approximation theorem (Theorem 5.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any function holomorphic in a neighborhood of a compact set K can be approximated uniformly on K by rational functions whose singularities lie in K^c. If K^c is connected, any such function can be approximated uniformly on K by polynomials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key ingredients: an integral representation of f on K by integrals over finitely many segments in K^c (Lemma 5.8), approximation of those integrals by Riemann sums giving rational functions with poles on segments (Lemma 5.9), and 'pushing' poles to infinity (Lemma 5.10) when K^c is connected to turn rational functions into polynomials. The necessity of K^c connected is shown by counterexamples such as f(z)=1/z on the unit circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral representation by contours in complement (Lemma 5.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in open Ω and K⊂Ω compact, there exist finitely many segments γ1,...,γN contained in Ω−K such that for all z∈K, f(z)= sum_{n=1}^N (1/2πi) ∫_{γn} f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct a grid of small squares intersecting K, take boundaries; interior square integrals cancel except for sides lying in Ω−K. This gives an explicit representation of f on K by integrals over segments in the complement, which is the starting point for approximation by rational functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation of segment integrals by rational functions (Lemma 5.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any segment γ contained in Ω−K, the integral γ f(ζ)/(ζ−z) dζ can be uniformly approximated on K by a sequence of rational functions with singularities on γ (via Riemann sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parametrize the segment and note the integrand is jointly continuous on K×[0,1]; choose δ for uniform continuity and approximate the integral by Riemann sums which are rational functions (finite sums of terms of the form f(γ(t_k))/(γ(t_k)−z)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pushing poles to infinity / approximating 1/(z−z0) by polynomials (Lemma 5.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If K^c is connected and z0∉K, then the function 1/(z−z0) can be approximated uniformly on K by polynomials (equivalently, one can approximate rational functions with poles in K^c by polynomials by 'moving' poles to infinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a path in K^c connecting z0 to a point z1 far away; expand geometric series uniformly on K to express 1/(z−z1) as power series and then bootstrap stepwise along a chain of nearby points on the curve to approximate 1/(z−z0) by polynomials in 1/(z−z1), then by polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: types of isolated singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated singularities of a holomorphic function are classified as removable singularities (can extend holomorphically), poles (function blows up like (z−z0)^{-n}), or essential singularities (wild oscillatory behavior; not removable or pole).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removable: 1/f holomorphic at the point after defining value 0; pole: 1/f has zero of finite order; essential: Laurent series has infinitely many negative terms. The behavior at each type guides extension and integration arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeros factorization (Theorem 1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in connected Ω, has a zero at z0 but is not identically zero, then there exists neighborhood U, a non-vanishing holomorphic g on U, and a unique positive integer n such that f(z)=(z−z0)^n g(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes zeros' multiplicity and is proved by examining the power series expansion and taking the first nonzero coefficient. Use to deduce local behavior and to understand poles/reciprocal functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pole representation (Theorem 1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a pole at z0, then in a neighborhood there exist a non-vanishing holomorphic h and a unique positive integer n such that f(z)=(z−z0)^{-n} h(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses the local structure near a pole: order n measures growth rate. Follows from applying Theorem 1.1 to 1/f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laurent expansion and principal part (Theorem 1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Near a pole of order n at z0, f has an expansion f(z)=a_{−n}/(z−z0)^n + ... + a_{−1}/(z−z0) + G(z), where G is holomorphic near z0; the principal part is the finite sum of negative-power terms and a_{−1} is the residue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal part captures obstruction to having a primitive in a deleted neighborhood; only the a_{−1} term contributes to integrals ∮ f around small circles about z0. Compute coefficients from local expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue at a simple pole
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a simple pole at z0, then res_{z0} f = lim_{z→z0} (z−z0) f(z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when integrand has simple poles; often simplifies residue calculations for rational functions or quotients where numerator and denominator are analytic and denominator has a simple zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue for higher-order poles (Theorem 1.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f has a pole of order n at z0, then res_{z0} f = (1/(n−1)!) lim_{z→z0} d^{n−1}/dz^{n−1} [ (z−z0)^n f(z) ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differentiation formula to compute residues for poles of order >1; expand (z−z0)^n f(z) as a Taylor series and extract coefficient of (z−z0)^{n−1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residue theorem (Theorem 2.1) and corollaries
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is holomorphic in an open set containing a closed contour γ and its interior except for finitely many poles z1,...,zN inside γ, then ∮_γ f(z) dz = 2πi ∑_{k=1}^N res_{z_k} f. In particular, this holds for circles and for 'toy contours' with positive orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by replacing integrals by sums of integrals over small circles around each pole (keyhole/multiple keyhole contours) and applying local residue calculation. Fundamental tool for evaluating complex integrals and real improper integrals via contour integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: compute improper real integrals by contour integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Many real improper integrals ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x) dx can be computed by extending f to the complex plane, choosing a family of contours γ_R so that lim_{R→∞} ∮_{γ_R} f(z) dz = ∫_{−∞}^{∞} f(x) dx, and applying the residue theorem to compute the contour integrals via residues of f inside γ_R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key choices: pick contour compatible with decay/growth of f (e.g., large semicircle in upper half-plane if integrand decays there); show arc integrals vanish as R→∞ (use bounds like |f(z)| ≤ const/|z|^2 on arcs); compute residues of enclosed poles. Examples provided: ∫ dx/(1+x^2)=π and ∫ e^{ax}/(1+e^x) dx = π / sin(π a) for 0<a<1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Morera's theorem to prove holomorphy across boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function is continuous on a region and its integrals over all triangles (or an appropriate family of contours) vanish, then it is holomorphic. This is used to check holomorphy at boundary points when gluing functions (e.g., in the symmetry principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In applications, adjust triangles slightly (raise vertices or split triangles) so they lie entirely in regions where f is already known to be holomorphic, take limits by continuity, then apply Morera's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topology condition for polynomial approximation on compact sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A necessary and sufficient topological condition for approximating holomorphic functions on a compact K by polynomials is that the complement K^c be connected; if K^c is not connected approximation by polynomials can fail (counterexample f(z)=1/z on unit circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies when Runge's theorem second part applies; when K^c is connected one can 'push' all poles to infinity converting rational approximants into polynomials.
